concepts.def: A cell that has its genetic material enclosed in a nucleus. Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic cells; they also have a cell membrane and cytoplasm.

A cell whose genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus. Bacterial cells are prokaryotic cells: they have cytoplasm and a cell membrane surrounded by a cell wall, they are much smaller than plant and animal cells, and their genetic material is a single DNA loop.
A small ring of DNA in the cytoplasm of a bacterial cell, separate from the single DNA loop. A bacterial cell may contain one or more plasmids.
The sub-cellular structure that encloses the genetic material of a plant or animal cell and controls the activities of the cell.
The structure that surrounds the cytoplasm of a cell and controls the passage of substances into and out of the cell.
The jelly-like part of a cell in which most of the cell's chemical reactions take place and in which the sub-cellular structures are found.

Sub-cellular structures in which aerobic respiration takes place, transferring the energy the cell needs to carry out its functions. Cells that need a great deal of energy, such as muscle cells, contain many mitochondria.
Sub-cellular structures where protein synthesis takes place: amino acids are joined together to make the proteins the cell needs.

A sub-cellular structure found in plant and algal cells that contains chlorophyll. The chlorophyll absorbs light so that the cell can carry out photosynthesis, so chloroplasts are found in plant cells that receive light rather than in every plant cell.
A space in the cytoplasm of a plant cell that is filled with cell sap. It is one of the parts plant cells often have in addition to the parts found in animal cells.
A layer made of cellulose that surrounds the cell membrane of plant and algal cells and strengthens the cell. Animal cells do not have a cell wall.
A cell whose structure enables it to carry out a particular function. Examples are sperm cells, nerve cells and muscle cells in animals, and root hair cells, xylem and phloem cells in plants.
A specialised plant cell in the root with a long, thin extension into the soil. The extension increases the surface area of the cell for absorbing water and mineral ions.

Specialised plant cells that form transport tissues. Xylem cells form hollow tubes with thickened walls that carry water and mineral ions from the roots; phloem cells form tubes with sieve plates that carry dissolved sugars through the plant.

The process in which a cell acquires different sub-cellular structures to enable it to carry out a certain function, so that it becomes a specialised cell. Most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage, while many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.
How many times larger an image is than the real object, calculated using magnification = size of image / size of real object. The image size and the real size must be measured in the same units.

The ability of a microscope to show two points that are close together as separate points. An electron microscope has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope, so it can be used to study cells in much finer detail.

The simple cell division by which bacteria multiply. If they have enough nutrients and a suitable temperature, bacteria can divide as often as once every 20 minutes, so the population doubles at each division.
The nutrients supplied for growing microorganisms. Bacteria can be grown in a nutrient broth solution, or as colonies on an agar gel plate.

The set of precautions used to prepare an uncontaminated culture. Petri dishes and culture media are sterilised before use; inoculating loops are sterilised by passing them through a flame; the lid of the Petri dish is secured with adhesive tape and the dish is stored upside down; and in school and college laboratories cultures are incubated at a maximum temperature of 25°C.

A culture that contains only the microorganism being studied, with no microorganisms from the air, the skin or the apparatus. Uncontaminated cultures are required for investigating the action of disinfectants and antibiotics.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a bacterial cell is correct?
options: Its genetic material is held inside a nucleus.
Its cell wall is made from cellulose fibres.
Its width is close to that of a cheek cell.
Its genetic material is a single DNA loop.
mcqs.explain: The genetic material of a bacterial cell is not enclosed in a nucleus: it is a single DNA loop, and there may also be one or more small rings of DNA called plasmids.

mcqs.q: A cheek cell is 6 × 10⁻⁵ m wide and a bacterial cell is 2 × 10⁻⁶ m wide. About how many times wider is the cheek cell?
options: About 3 times wider
About 300 times wider
About 30 times wider
About 0.03 times wider
mcqs.explain: 6 × 10⁻⁵ divided by 2 × 10⁻⁶ is 3 × 10¹, so the cheek cell is about 30 times wider. This is the order of magnitude difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

mcqs.q: A muscle cell contains large numbers of mitochondria. What is the function of these mitochondria?
options: To transfer energy by aerobic respiration
To make energy needed for contraction
To join amino acids into new proteins
To store the glucose used in exercise
mcqs.explain: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place, transferring the energy the cell needs. A muscle cell needs a great deal of energy, so its structure includes many mitochondria.

mcqs.q: Which parts are found in most animal cells?
options: Cytoplasm, ribosomes and a cellulose wall
Cytoplasm, mitochondria and cell sap
Cytoplasm, ribosomes and mitochondria
Cytoplasm, ribosomes and a large vacuole
mcqs.explain: Most animal cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes, so all three parts listed here are present.

mcqs.q: Which statement about plant cells is correct?
options: Their cell walls are found in animals too.
Their cell walls are made of cellulose.
Their chloroplasts are in every plant cell.
Their vacuoles are found in animals too.
mcqs.explain: Plant and algal cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell.

mcqs.q: A plant cell is 0.06 mm long. On a drawing of the cell, the nucleus is about one tenth of the length of the cell. What is the best estimate of the real diameter of the nucleus?
options: 0.6 mm
mcqs.explain: The estimate from the drawing is that the nucleus is one tenth of the cell length, so its real diameter is 0.06 mm / 10 = 0.006 mm. This judges the relative size of a sub-cellular structure.

mcqs.q: Root hair cells have a long, thin extension that reaches out into the soil. How does this help the cell to carry out its function?
options: It makes the cell larger so it can work faster.
It exposes the chloroplasts to more sunlight.
It allows a thicker cellulose wall to form.
It increases the surface area for absorption.
mcqs.explain: The structure of the root hair cell relates to its function in the plant: the extension gives a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.

mcqs.q: Which statement about cell differentiation is correct?
options: Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage.
Most plant cells differentiate at an early stage.
Most cells differentiate by growing to a bigger size.
Most animal cells differentiate to repair damage.
mcqs.explain: As an organism develops, cells differentiate to form different types of cell, and most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage.

mcqs.q: In a mature animal, what is cell division mainly used for?
options: Cell division has stopped in mature animals.
Cell division makes the cells grow larger.
Cell division repairs and replaces cells.
Cell division continues as the animal grows.
mcqs.explain: In mature animals, cell division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.

mcqs.q: Why can an electron microscope be used to study cells in much finer detail than a light microscope?
options: It magnifies the image very many more times.
It has higher magnification and resolution.
It finds the real size from the image size.
It uses a much stronger lens to enlarge cells.
mcqs.explain: An electron microscope has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope, so it can be used to study cells in much finer detail.

mcqs.q: The image of a cell is 10 mm wide. The real cell is 0.05 mm wide. What is the magnification?
mcqs.explain: magnification = size of image / size of real object = 10 mm / 0.05 mm = 200. Both measurements are in the same units, so the magnification has no units.

mcqs.q: One bacterium divides once every 20 minutes. How many bacteria will there be after 2 hours?
options: 12 bacteria
64 bacteria
7 bacteria
120 bacteria
mcqs.explain: There are 6 divisions in 2 hours at one division every 20 minutes, and the population doubles each time, so the number is 1 × 2⁶ = 64.

mcqs.q: One bacterium divides once every 20 minutes. What is the number of bacteria after 5 hours, expressed in standard form?
mcqs.explain: 5 hours gives 15 divisions, so the number is 2¹⁵ = 32 768, which is 3.3 × 10⁴ to two significant figures in standard form.

mcqs.q: Why should cultures be incubated at a maximum temperature of 25°C in a school laboratory?
options: It reduces the growth of harmful pathogens.
It is the temperature for fastest growth.
It stops condensation forming on the lid.
It matches the body temperature of humans.
mcqs.explain: In school and college laboratories cultures are incubated at a maximum of 25°C, because this reduces the likelihood of growing pathogens that could harm people.

mcqs.q: Why is a Petri dish stored upside down after the agar gel has been inoculated?
options: To stop the agar falling out of the dish.
To stop condensation dripping onto the agar.
To keep the culture warm enough to grow.
To hold the lid firmly against the agar.
mcqs.explain: With the dish upside down, condensation collects on the lid below the agar gel and cannot drip onto its surface, so the culture stays uncontaminated.

mcqs.q: A clear area around a colony on an agar plate is 20 mm across. What is its cross-sectional area?
options: 314 mm²
1257 mm²
63 mm²
31.4 mm²
mcqs.explain: The radius is half of 20 mm, so r = 10 mm and the cross-sectional area is πr² = π × 10² = 314 mm².
